dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is four days old, and Mike, you're off work today to help Kelly at home, which is exactly where the day should be spent. Overnight, the Ukraine aid-centre death toll rose to 42 ahead of next week's Abu Dhabi peace talks, oil fell for a fourth straight day on hopes the midterm result pushes Washington toward an Iran deal, and the post-election map settled: Democrats hold both chambers of Congress, and Ohio has a governor-elect in Amy Acton and a returning senator in Sherrod Brown. The Cavs lost the rematch in Oklahoma City last night, 124-116, despite Donovan Mitchell's late flurry, and Jarrett Allen left early with a knee knock — they're home Friday against Philadelphia and Saturday against the Knicks. Solon stays cloudy and dry today with a high near 61°, but rain and a sharp cooldown arrive Friday into Saturday, so today is the day for any errands. If energy somehow allows tonight, Hadestown is at Playhouse Square at 7:30 PM.

weekBrief.text: Benji's first full week at home is a settle-in week: he was born Sunday, came home Tuesday, saw his pediatrician Wednesday, and now gets a quiet house while Mike takes Thursday off to help Kelly. Solon's weather turns with the weekend — cloudy and dry near 61° Thursday, then rain and a sharp cooldown Friday (49°) and Saturday (46°), clearing Sunday and rebounding into the 50s and low 60s through Tuesday. The week's best grocery move is a Thanksgiving stock-up: Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb, and one bird covers a roast dinner now plus soup and chili later. If energy allows, the Cavs are home twice at Rocket Arena — Friday against Philadelphia and Saturday against the Knicks — alongside Hadestown at Playhouse Square on Thursday, the free Día de Muertos celebration on Saturday, Ohio State hosting Oregon Saturday afternoon, and the Browns at New Orleans on Sunday.

Two tankers and a tug catch fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
items.summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz after using routes Tehran calls unauthorised. One tanker was said to have struck a naval mine south of the strait, while a supertanker caught fire leaving the waterway and a tug that came to help it also burned.

The report follows a claim a day earlier that four tankers were destroyed after hitting mines and two other vessels were seized. Separately, Britain's maritime trade operations agency said it had received a report of a tanker struck by two unidentified projectiles north of Qatar, with the crew's status not yet confirmed.

Hormuz is the main exit route for Gulf oil, so repeated mine and fire incidents raise shipping, insurance and supply risks at a moment when crude had been falling on hopes of an Iran deal. Iran gave no casualty or damage figures for Thursday's incidents, and independent confirmation is still limited.

Watch for confirmation from shipping agencies, whether tanker companies pause transits, and how oil prices react through the afternoon.

items.title: Bank of England raises rates to 4% for the first time since 2023 and warns more may come
items.summary:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate to 4% from 3.75% on Thursday, its first increase in more than three years. The vote was 8 to 1, and the lone dissenter wanted an even bigger move to 4.25%, arguing the bank had been too slow to reassure markets about inflation.

British inflation was 3.5% in September, and the bank now expects it to peak near 4.8% next spring and not return to its 2% target until late 2028 — about six months later than it forecast in July. In a worse case, with oil around $130 a barrel, inflation could reach above 6% next year. Growth forecasts were actually revised up, helped by spending on artificial intelligence.

Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be read as the start of an endless run of hikes, but that unless the Middle East conflict settles, it is unlikely to be the last one either. That is a direct cost-of-living problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government, with real household incomes set to fall this year and next.

The next decision comes on December 17. Watch whether support grows for larger hikes, and how markets price the path for 2027.

items.title: Ukraine hits Russian refineries again as a U.S.-bound Russian diesel deal comes into focus
items.summary:
Ukraine renewed its strikes on Russian oil refineries overnight, with the large Ryazan plant southeast of Moscow appearing to come under attack in a big drone strike. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery hit this week, after Yaroslavl on Monday, ending a pause in that campaign. Ryazan's governor said power was restored and industrial fires were contained.

Ukrainian strikes this year have knocked out large amounts of processing capacity in western Russia, caused fuel shortages at home, and pushed Moscow to ban fuel exports from April. Part of a diesel export ban was later lifted under an October deal with Washington, struck when President Trump was trying to calm diesel prices before the midterms.

The shipping picture is murky: at least six Russian diesel cargoes have signalled transatlantic voyages, two appeared to change course after heading for the U.S. Atlantic coast, and none has yet arrived under the deal. Analysts say a first cargo could reach New York this weekend, but unloading is not guaranteed given regulatory and sanctions questions. The Kremlin denied any link between tanker movements and the election result.

Watch for confirmation of the Ryazan damage, whether that New York cargo actually discharges, and whether the new Democratic Congress moves to block the diesel deal.

items.title: France keeps a patrol plane in the Black Sea longer after deadly attacks on cargo ships
items.summary:
A French Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft based in Romania will stay several weeks longer than planned, its commander said Thursday. The plane, at the Mihail Kogalniceanu air base since October 18, had been due to leave on Friday. It hunts submarines, warships, sea drones and mines, though it cannot shoot drones down itself.

Romania and Bulgaria asked NATO for help after a series of deadly strikes on merchant ships near their coasts. At least nine cargo ships were hit in October, with about 34 sailors dead or missing. The French crew detected the three sea drones that sank a Greek-owned container ship off Bulgaria on October 28, and its warning an hour ahead let that crew escape unharmed.

The extension shows how the Russia-Ukraine war at sea is spilling toward NATO's eastern flank and threatening grain and oil shipping through the Black Sea. Russia has denied targeting Ukraine's neighbours.

Watch for further ship attacks, whether other allies extend their deployments, and how NATO's planned counter-drone investment is used.

items.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong is sentenced to another 10 years in prison
items.summary:
Hong Kong's High Court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, 30, to 10 years in prison on Thursday for conspiring to collude with foreign forces under the national security law imposed by Beijing. Wong had pleaded guilty in September, and the judge reduced a 13-year starting point because of that plea.

Prosecutors said Wong worked with exiled activist Nathan Law and others in 2020 to seek foreign sanctions and blockades, including lobbying American politicians. Only about two months of the new sentence runs alongside his current term, so his time in prison now stretches toward late 2036.

Wong has been in custody since November 2020 and was already serving a sentence from the mass subversion case involving 47 democracy figures, with release previously expected in January 2027. He was the teenage face of the protest movements of 2012 and 2014, and he is the only activist prosecuted twice under the security law. Hong Kong's leader called the offences extremely serious, while supporters camped outside court.

Watch for international reaction, any appeal, and whether the case further complicates Hong Kong's pitch as an open financial hub.

items.title: North Korea tests a new air-defence missile and stages a cruise missile drill
items.summary:
North Korea test-fired a newly designed air-defence missile system and staged a strategic cruise missile strike drill on Wednesday, state media reported Thursday. Officials said the test checked the missile's technical performance, new materials, guidance, and ability to identify and track targets, while a cruise missile unit struck a mock airport target.

The report matched a South Korean military statement that Pyongyang had fired multiple missiles toward the sea from its east coast. It was the fourth North Korean weapons launch in about a month, and early data suggested several different missile types were involved.

Analysts looking at images released by Pyongyang said one cruise missile appeared to carry a cluster warhead, and that the new air-defence missile's guidance section resembles Russia's S-400 system. That resemblance raises fresh questions about Russian technology reaching North Korea.

Watch for the response from the United States, South Korea and Japan, any further launches, and whether a Russian link is ever confirmed.

items.title: Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat on Wednesday, in a long post on X that put clear distance between him and President Trump. He said voters who backed the ticket in 2024 crossed over or stayed home because they were angry, not because turnout collapsed.

Vance listed what he said those voters want: an end to the war, a focus on the cost of living and inflation, an America First approach, and a changed relationship with Israel. He challenged defenders of the war to argue that losing the Senate for years was worth it. Trump was more measured, saying Iran was part of the result, telling reporters he did the right thing and would do it again.

Exit polling cited in coverage put the cost of living and government corruption ahead of the war as voter concerns, with fuel and grocery prices surging during the conflict and under tariffs. The war began in late February and has lasted about eight months.

The post reads as the first clear positioning move for 2028. Watch whether Vance's list turns into a policy push inside the White House, and how other Republican hopefuls frame their own postmortems.

items.title: Trump backs Hegseth as Republicans turn on him and an impeachment vote nears
items.summary:
President Trump said he intends to keep Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, even as many Republicans privately blame Hegseth for selling the Iran war as a quick win. At the same time, the House could vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as next week.

Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky says he will trigger an impeachment vote when Congress returns on November 9, and several Republican sources expect it to pass the House. His articles, first introduced in September, allege among other things that Hegseth continued hostilities against Iran beyond the War Powers window without authorisation from Congress. Massie said the only way he stands down is if Hegseth resigns.

Republicans speaking anonymously said Hegseth oversold how easily Iran would fold, kept pushing escalation, and has few friends on Capitol Hill. Trump said Hegseth is doing a very good job, and the Pentagon said he is fully committed to serving out the term. Impeachment by the House would still need a two-thirds Senate vote to remove him, and the Senate stays Republican until January.

Watch the House vote next week, how many Republicans break ranks, and whether Trump reconsiders if the House impeaches his defense secretary.

items.title: Trump demands Alaska hand the 'fake Dan Sullivan' votes to Senator Dan Sullivan
items.summary:
President Trump posted on Truth Social on Thursday demanding that votes cast for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — whom he called the fake Dan Sullivan — be given instead to Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, and that the Alaska Senate election be declared over.

The actual count is extremely close. Democrat Mary Peltola leads by roughly 637 votes in first-choice counting, with both leading candidates just under 48%, the second Sullivan at about 1.7%, and another Republican at about 2.3%. About a quarter of ballots were still uncounted, and mail ballots can keep arriving for days.

The demand reverses Trump's election-night statement that he would accept the results. The Justice Department sued in October to block certification if Peltola narrowly wins, claiming the second Sullivan was recruited to confuse voters; a federal judge dismissed that suit before Election Day, and the department is appealing. Alaska's own courts allowed Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, listed without a party to distinguish him.

There is no sign Alaska officials will reassign anyone's votes — that is not how the count works. The race helps decide the final size of the Democrats' new Senate majority. Ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if nobody tops 50%, with certification on November 25.

items.title: Speaker Mike Johnson steps aside; Scalise and Jim Jordan race to lead House Republicans
items.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson announced Wednesday that he will not seek to lead House Republicans in the new Congress, after Democrats regained the House majority. He told staff that morning and wrote to colleagues that leadership had demanded significant sacrifices from his family; the letter did not mention the defeat. He stays on as speaker until the new House is sworn in in January and keeps the Louisiana seat he won again on Tuesday.

Two contenders launched bids the same day. Majority Leader Steve Scalise, Johnson's number two, called the result far worse than expected. Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, a founder of the Freedom Caucus, has blamed current leadership in part for the loss. Both men tried and failed to win the speakership in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy's ouster.

The winner will lead the minority against incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries and shape the party's two-year rebuild and its message heading toward 2028. Trump has said he will stay out of the race.

Candidate declarations are due by noon Friday, and House Republicans vote by secret ballot on Tuesday, November 10.

items.title: Jeffries launches his bid to become the first Black Speaker, with a 100-day affordability plan
items.summary:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries formally launched his bid on Wednesday to become the 57th Speaker of the House — and the first Black Speaker — in a letter to the incoming Congress. He framed the bid around affordability, accountability and American values.

For the first 100 days, Jeffries listed five priorities: reversing Medicaid cuts, restoring food assistance funding, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, wiping out Trump's tariffs, and stopping the war in Iran, which he called a reckless war of choice. He blamed tariffs and the war for driving up everyday costs, and his caucus has set up working groups on housing, health care, groceries, fuel and caregiving.

Democrats are on track for at least 255 House seats. Almost everything on the list faces a Trump veto, and Democrats do not have the two-thirds majorities needed to override one — so the agenda works both as an opening governing programme and as a contrast for 2028, backed by the oversight power that comes with controlling committees.

The Speaker vote happens on January 3 when the new Congress convenes. Watch for any resistance from Jeffries' left flank, and which item Democrats actually bring to the floor first.

items.title: Mississippi's Senate race is still too close to call
items.summary:
Mississippi's Senate race remained too close to call on Thursday, with Democrat Scott Colom narrowly ahead of Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the most Republican states in the country. Recent counts put Colom ahead by somewhere between a few dozen votes and about 1,700, out of nearly a million cast, with both candidates at about 49%.

About 15,000 affidavit and provisional ballots still need to be checked, according to Colom's campaign — a figure election officials have not independently confirmed. Absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive until November 10. Mississippi has no automatic recount law for a race like this, so a recount would have to be sought through a judge.

A Colom win would make him Mississippi's first Democratic senator since John C. Stennis's era and its first Black senator since Reconstruction. Together with Alaska, this race decides how large the Democrats' new Senate majority will be.

Watch the ballot vetting over the coming days and the legal fight both sides are already preparing for.

items.title: Tech rout deepens as chip stocks plunge and the Nasdaq nears a correction
items.summary:
Technology stocks headed for their worst day since June on Thursday. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell as much as 11% intraday — its worst showing since March 2020 — and the Nasdaq fell as much as 5%, a move that would confirm a correction, meaning a drop of 10% from last month's record high.

More than a dozen large tech names fell by double digits, including AMD, SanDisk, Micron, Dell and Marvell. The selling follows a bruising month since the Nasdaq's October 6 record, tighter financing for companies building data centres, weak results from Qualcomm and Arm, and Tuesday's local votes limiting data-centre construction.

Analysts are split. Some call this emotional de-leveraging after a huge run; others say growth investors are handing off to value investors and that the returns on enormous AI spending are now being questioned, with reports of big companies trimming AI budgets.

Watch whether the Nasdaq closes in correction territory, whether bargain hunters return as they did on Wednesday, and how the new Congress affects the AI building boom.

items.title: Qualcomm falls sharply as smartphone chip sales miss forecasts
items.summary:
Qualcomm shares dropped more than 9% on Thursday, putting the company on track to lose over $17 billion in market value, after sales of smartphone chips missed Wall Street's estimates. Revenue in its handset division, its largest business, fell 26% to $5.14 billion, pulling total chip sales down 8%.

The wider phone market is weak: global smartphone shipments fell 20% in the September quarter to a 14-year low, as demand for AI data-centre memory pushed memory prices up and made devices more expensive. Qualcomm's guidance for the current quarter also came in slightly below expectations and assumed no further chip sales to Apple.

There are offsets. Qualcomm expects about $650 million from data-centre products this quarter, ahead of estimates, and its automotive business is growing. But at least eight brokerages cut their price targets on Thursday, saying the new businesses have not yet replaced the handset and Apple revenue being lost.

Watch whether data-centre and car growth can carry the company in 2027, and how much of the memory cost phone makers pass on to buyers.

items.title: AMD posts a record $13.4 billion quarter as data-centre sales nearly double
items.summary:
AMD reported revenue of $13.4 billion for its third quarter, up 45% from a year earlier and above the top of its own guidance, with earnings per share up sharply as well. Data-centre revenue hit a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year over year, driven by its server processors and the launch of its newest AI graphics processors. That business is now about 64% of everything AMD sells.

The rest of the company was mixed. Embedded products grew, client chips grew modestly, but gaming revenue fell 40% on weaker console and graphics sales. AMD guided to about $17 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and said server revenue could double again in 2027, even as it plans for PC shipments to fall.

Big AI names including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle were named as running workloads on AMD's first rack-scale systems. If AMD and Intel both hit their guidance, AMD's quarter could exceed Intel's for the first time — a symbolic changing of the guard.

None of that protected the stock on Thursday: AMD was among the double-digit fallers in the chip rout. Watch fourth-quarter delivery and whether data-centre growth keeps offsetting gaming and PC weakness.

items.title: Humanoid robot maker Agility Robotics starts trading on the Nasdaq
items.summary:
Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker AGLT, after completing a merger that brought in about $465 million in gross capital at a $2.5 billion pre-money valuation. The financing included backing led by Foxconn. The money is earmarked for filling orders, expanding deployments, scaling production of its Digit robot, and developing its robotics platform.

Agility calls itself the first publicly listed U.S. company focused purely on humanoid robots with real commercial work underway. Its Digit robots have logged more than 65,000 hours, including moving over 100,000 totes at a GXO warehouse in Georgia, with deployments also at Schaeffler and Toyota in Canada.

The valuation rests on the future, not the present: revenue in 2025 was only $1.8 million against a net loss of roughly $138 million. The company points to more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit 5, though those depend on milestones and are not yet revenue. Its Oregon factory is designed to build up to 10,000 robots a year.

Watch AGLT's first trading days, and whether Digit 5 commitments turn into deployed, paid robots when early customer access starts in 2027.

items.title: Meta buys AI coding startup Conductor as the coding-agent race heats up
items.summary:
Meta has acquired Conductor, a startup whose tool lets engineers run and manage several AI coding agents at once, in a deal first reported Wednesday. No price was disclosed. Conductor's founder confirmed the team is joining Meta, where they will work inside its superintelligence group.

Conductor launched in July 2025, raised $22 million earlier this year, and built a user base reported at more than 100,000. Its software runs agents from different labs side by side in separate workspaces so engineers can review and merge their work. Existing users are on a clock: new sign-ups stopped Wednesday, the cloud service goes read-only on November 13 and shuts down on November 20, while the Mac app keeps working into early 2027.

On the same day, OpenAI confirmed plans to acquire Pierre Computer, whose code-storage tools are already used inside its Codex product — a move aimed at the ground Microsoft's GitHub occupies. Together the deals show the big labs buying the workflow layer around coding agents, not just building models.

Watch whether Meta folds Conductor into its own coding tools, and whether the Pierre deal clears regulators.

items.title: OpenAI says its AI agents found 948 ways to gain root access to Linux
items.summary:
OpenAI reported this week that an automated security pipeline, run in mid-October with an upcoming specialist model, produced working exploits for 948 distinct flaws in the Linux kernel — bugs that let a low-privilege user already on a machine seize full root control. The system also drafted candidate patches for each one.

The scale is the story. The pipeline produced more than 2,300 candidate findings, reproduced over 1,700 vulnerabilities, and built more than 1,100 working exploits, which were then grouped into the 948 unique cases. The run cost about $1.2 million in computing credits — roughly $1,279 per distinct flaw — and tests ran in controlled virtual machines with human review before anything went to maintainers.

Important limits: this is local escalation, not a remote break-in by itself, and drafted patches are not shipped fixes. Maintainers still have to review and accept them, and whether any given system is affected depends on its kernel version and settings. The results are vendor-reported and have not been independently reproduced.

Watch how many patches are accepted upstream, how many flaws get formal CVE listings, and whether maintainer review becomes the bottleneck as AI generates credible security findings at this volume.

items.title: Gunman kills a woman at a Citibank campus near Tampa before a guard stops him
items.summary:
A gunman drove a car through a fence at Citibank's sprawling Tampa-area campus on Wednesday, crashed into an outdoor area where employees were eating lunch, and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman, authorities said. About 3,200 people were at work on the campus at the time.

An armed Citibank security guard confronted the attacker inside a building cafeteria about four minutes after the first 911 calls, before deputies arrived. The two exchanged fire and the guard fatally wounded the gunman, who was pronounced dead at a hospital. The guard was wounded, and four other people were treated for injuries that were not life-threatening.

Investigators have not given a motive and have not said whether the gunman knew the woman he killed. Names were withheld pending notification of relatives, and hundreds of deputies and other responders flooded the business park in Brandon, east of Tampa.

Watch for the identifications, any stated motive, and what investigators determine about how the other victims were hurt.

items.title: Republicans press Trump to change course after the midterm rout
items.summary:
Republican allies and strategists pressed President Trump on Wednesday to shake up his staff, restore discipline, and drop the policies they blame for the midterm loss — above all the Iran war and tariffs. Democrats now gain the power to block legislation, investigate the administration, and challenge nominees.

Inside the White House, senior aides were bracing for departures, possible Cabinet changes, and congressional investigations, with one official describing morale as as low as it can get. That official said internal polling had warned six weeks before the election that both chambers were at risk, but Trump refused to change course on Iran. A veteran Republican strategist called the result a huge disaster and said Trump needs to clean house.

Trump himself gave reporters an impromptu tour of the White House ballroom construction on Wednesday and called it relaxing, and told Fox News he did not see the result as a hit on him. He still holds executive power and has spent months preparing orders on immigration, tariffs, housing and federal spending that do not need Congress.

Watch for actual staff or Cabinet departures during the lame-duck session, and whether Trump doubles down through executive action instead.

items.title: Los Angeles mayor is projected to fall, with council member Nithya Raman ahead
items.summary:
Decision Desk HQ projected Wednesday evening that City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in Los Angeles, with Raman leading by about 26,000 votes — roughly 51.7% to 48.3% — in the county count. Bass had led in early returns on Tuesday before Raman moved ahead as more ballots were counted.

The race is a projection, not a certification. The Associated Press had not called it, ballots postmarked by Election Day can still arrive for days, and Bass had not conceded. Both candidates are Democrats who advanced from a June primary; Bass's standing had fallen after the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, and a final poll had the two tied.

Raman entered the race hours before the filing deadline, shortly after endorsing Bass, and won backing from the local Democratic Socialists chapter. She would be the city's first socialist mayor, its first Asian-American mayor, and its second woman in the job.

Whoever wins runs a budget of about $14 billion and inherits homelessness, housing costs, recovery from the Palisades Fire, strained city services, and preparations for the 2028 Summer Olympics. County updates continue through mid-November, with certification due later this month.

items.title: Voters backed data-centre limits in 44 of 45 community ballots
items.summary:
Voters in 44 of the 45 American communities with a direct data-centre question on Tuesday's ballot chose to restrict, pause or ban large facilities. The one exception was Harwood, North Dakota, which voted to let a review process go forward. Different trackers count the measures slightly differently, but every count shows a near-sweep for restrictions.

Ohio had about 20 of the measures on its own. In Sunbury, 78% of voters backed a ban on facilities over 25 megawatts, halting a proposed Amazon-backed project put at $2 billion, and bans passed by similarly wide margins in places like Granville, Pataskala and Upper Sandusky. Across all the ballots, the restriction side took about 73% of the combined vote.

Opponents campaigned on noise, water use, electricity demand, higher utility bills, and how few permanent jobs these sites create relative to their size. Technology companies and their allies heavily outspent local campaigns and still lost almost everywhere.

One bank estimate cited in market coverage puts about 30% of expected U.S. data-centre additions for 2028 at risk from construction pauses. Watch whether legislatures or courts override local bans, and whether the big cloud companies shift building to friendlier states or generate their own power.

items.title: Elon Musk's record $474 million in election spending bought him little
items.summary:
Elon Musk spent about $474 million backing Republican causes in this election cycle — more than any non-candidate donor has ever spent in a single cycle — and Republicans still lost both chambers of Congress. Total midterm spending is projected at a record $11.9 billion, about 30% above 2022.

His biggest single bet failed most visibly. Musk put at least $45 million into the Texas Senate race behind Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico. Money also flowed into races in Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota, and records show spending continued right up to the day before polls closed. On Tuesday night, Musk joked on X that his election-interfering space lasers did not work.

Musk channelled most of the money through America PAC, which he founded in 2024, and the Senate Leadership Fund. The 40 largest donors overall gave $2.4 billion by mid-October, a record pace, and super PACs accounted for more than half of all spending recorded by then.

The return on the money is now the question: Musk's companies, Tesla and SpaceX, face a new Democratic Congress inclined to scrutinise government contracts. Final totals will only settle once the last campaign finance reports are filed.

items.title: DeWine says he won't back stripping Acton's power as she launches her transition
items.summary:
Governor Mike DeWine said Thursday that he does not think it is appropriate for the legislature to dramatically change the governor's powers before Amy Acton takes over, and that no governor of either party would approve such a move. He was speaking at a post-election Ohio Chamber of Commerce conference.

The comments answer speculation that Republican lawmakers might use the December lame-duck session to weaken the executive branch before January — a tactic the party previously used against DeWine himself during COVID. Incoming Senate President Bill Reineke said Senate Republicans have had no group discussions about limiting the governor's power and that he called Acton to congratulate her, while a Democratic senator argued Acton should be ready to threaten budget vetoes if lawmakers try.

DeWine and his wife met Acton and her husband at the governor's residence on Wednesday. Acton formally launched her transition on Thursday and picked John Haseley, a former chief of staff to Governor Ted Strickland, to run it. Democrats also broke the Republicans' veto-proof supermajority in the Ohio House on Tuesday, which strengthens her hand.

Acton is sworn in on January 11. Watch the lame-duck session for any late moves on governor powers despite DeWine's warning.

items.title: What Acton means for Ohio schools: a voucher-reform fight and a lame-duck watch
items.summary:
Amy Acton campaigned on reforming Ohio's EdChoice voucher programme, which she described as sending taxpayer money to private schools with little accountability, and on fully funding public schools under the bipartisan formula first approved in 2021. Voucher spending in Ohio has now passed $1.4 billion and faces court challenges, while about one in five public schools faces financial uncertainty.

The Statehouse math changed on Tuesday. Republicans fall below the 60-seat Ohio House supermajority they have held since 2013, so they can no longer override a governor's veto on their own — Acton's veto becomes a real lever in next summer's budget fight. Public-education advocates welcomed the result, while a leading school-choice voice predicted a compromise that adds public funding while largely preserving choice.

The risk window is before January. A pending bill would force under-enrolled public school buildings to close, be sold, or convert to charters, and it could move during lame duck while the current supermajority and Governor DeWine are still in place.

Watch the lame-duck calendar, and then Acton's first budget for how much of the 2021 funding formula she actually restores.

items.title: How Northeast Ohio voted: levies pass, charter limits pass, and the 7th District flips
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County voters passed Issue 10, the developmental disabilities levy, with nearly 63%, and Issue 11, the health and human services levy, with about 60%. Together they add about $166.50 a year for every $100,000 of property value. Voters also approved charter changes limiting some county executive powers.

Democrat Courtney Scheff beat Republican Mike Gallagher 53% to 47% in County Council District 5, which leaves Cuyahoga County Council with no Republicans at all. In the 7th Congressional District, Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union iron worker, unseated Representative Max Miller with about 53% of the vote. More than 1.7 million Ohioans voted early, a record for a governor's election year, and results are certified on November 24.

The same Cleveland roundup flags two city items to follow: federal housing officials rejected Cleveland's $7.8 million lead-cleanup grant after a risk review, and the city is seeking a debrief and checking its appeal options; and the foreclosure auction of downtown's Huntington Building at 925 Euclid Avenue was pushed to November 10, with about $40.1 million in defaulted loans and unpaid taxes attached to the property.

Watch the certification, the lead-grant appeal, and the Huntington Building auction next week.

items.title: Ohio voters lock voter photo ID into the state constitution
items.summary:
Ohio's Issue 3, the only statewide ballot issue, passed 65% to 35% on Tuesday, writing the state's voter photo ID requirement into the Ohio Constitution. In practice nothing changes today: Ohio has required photo ID for in-person voting by law since 2023.

What changes is durability. Because the requirement now sits in the constitution, weakening it would take another statewide vote rather than a simple change in state law. The amendment does not itself require photo ID for mail voting, but it does allow lawmakers to impose that by passing a new law — something they tried and failed to do earlier this year.

The measure reached the ballot at the urging of Vivek Ramaswamy and, in a notable break from traditional Democratic positioning, Acton supported it too. Supporters point to broad public backing for voter ID; critics call the amendment unnecessary given the existing law and the lack of evidence of widespread fraud.

Watch whether lawmakers now move on mail-voting ID rules, knowing the constitutional ground has shifted under that debate.

items.title: Rock Hall expansion: only the Haslam Auditorium opens on November 22
items.summary:
A correction issued early Thursday clarified that only the Haslam Auditorium portion of the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's expansion will open on November 22 — not the full expansion, as earlier reporting suggested. The auditorium is the expansion's public-facing community space, it will be free to enter, and visitors will come in through a new entrance past a lakeside garden.

The triangular extension is the Rock Hall's largest construction project since its 1991 groundbreaking. When the whole project is complete, exhibition space will almost double, food space grows, and a new concert and events venue will anchor the addition. Fundraising for the project was overwhelmingly local.

The opening lands while the lakefront around it changes fast: the Browns are bound for Brook Park, the Port of Cleveland is in a major renovation, and the city's land-bridge plans for the shoreway are advancing.

Watch for the full expansion's opening date, and how the free auditorium is programmed once it opens later this month.

items.title: More than 1,100 chinchillas surrendered by a Northwest Ohio breeder after a federal case
items.summary:
The owner of R&R Chinchilla, near Jenera in Hancock County, has surrendered more than 1,100 chinchillas in total — roughly 800 earlier under a court order and the remaining 300 or so under a consent decree endorsed on November 2. The rescue was completed on November 3.

The Justice Department says inspectors documented untreated medical conditions and heavy fecal accumulation, and that about 800 animals had been hidden in a second building for years to avoid inspection. The operation had bred chinchillas for over 40 years, selling to laboratories and the pet trade, and had been cited for Animal Welfare Act violations repeatedly since 2022.

Humane World for Animals led the removal and took the animals to an undisclosed location for treatment and exams. Under the court agreements, the owner's federal licence is permanently revoked and he is barred from regulated animal activity. A county criminal investigation into possible Ohio cruelty violations is described as ongoing.

Watch for the county case, and for where the rescued animals are placed once they are treated.

baby.tip: Day 4 tip — diaper math: by today Benji should be having at least 3–4 wet diapers and several stools a day, and the counts should keep climbing toward 6+ wet diapers by day five or six. Keep the little log going on the fridge or phone; it's the simplest feeding check there is, and it's exactly what his pediatrician's office will ask about. If a full day looks low, that's a call-the-pediatrician question, not a wait-and-see one.
baby.fact: At four days old, Benji can only focus clearly on things about 8 to 12 inches from his face — which is, not coincidentally, about the distance to a parent's face during a feeding. High-contrast patterns and your faces are basically his favourite channel right now.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for Day 4: the first tummy-time minute — a short, supervised session on a firm surface while Benji is awake and calm. One minute counts as a win, and a Moose-supervised (from a polite distance) session counts double.
